**The saddest ten days**

Easter Monday, March 26, 1951

It must’ve been 10 o'clock in the morning when Dr Anne Casey, 36, hauled herself out of bed and waddled over to the mirror-image bedroom occupied by her husband, Dr Austie Casey, 52. As soon as she opened the door, she let out a yelp, to the horror of the children and everyone else in the house, because she had found him dead to the world. It was Austie's third heart attack and he slipped away in his sleep, worn out perhaps from the festivities of the Easter weekend.

Anne had been sleeping in the other room because she was due to have the baby any day now, and the complications had already begun. There was still hope too, even if the odds were against her. Laura had been a miracle and was a ruddy two year old now, the first Rhesus baby in Ireland to survive. She got the all-important blood transfusion that had only recently become available. Austie must have had to muscle his way through his medical contacts in Dublin and managed to pull together a team who could save the baby. The chances of survival were lower for subsequent babies and Austie's clout would have been needed to pull together the right team for this coming birth. Alas, nine days later, the young widow would bear a still born baby, Joseph Patrick Casey, 0, and his little body would be buried beside his father in the loose soil of the family grave.

Jane was **five** and remembers it all. Richard was six and Michael, the eldest, was eight, his father's pride and joy, and now he would have to become the man of the house. It must have taken time for Anne to came to, then she called for help from the nanny. When no one came, Anne had to traipse downstairs, her flock trailing behind her, to ask the maids where that aul wan was gone to. They said she was gone to Mass. The aul dragon. She's always gone to mass when she's wanted. Anne struggled back up the stairs and Michael went in with his mammy to see his father, and him there, gone.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The early years had been idyllic for the Casey family. The war was over and the world was opening up. Michael Augustine Casey had long been the Medical Officer for the county town of Dungarvan in West Waterford, along the southern coast of Ireland. Incredibly, he was also the managing director of the town's two factories, both of which he had helped set up. In his latter years, he found himself and his beautiful wife travelling all around America, buying machines and visiting family in Chicago and Los Angeles. Business was booming now and the men of Dungarvan and surroundings areas had steady work, all year round, largely thanks to Austie Casey. Ireland in the 1950s hadn't happened yet and the mood was still good. No sooner were the lovers back from The States and they went on a cruise to Portugal and Madeira. They had a nanny and three maids to help them raise the children.

Soon the children would be like stray cats. With no father, their mother would be flat out as a dispensary doctor, working like a dog to keep the whole thing going, thanks to the paltry stipend she received in accordance with Austie's second will, which had been changed after one of his heart attacks. Soon enough, Austie's siblings all began to drop, some of them afflicted by the same heart condition. In ten years' time, only one of the six was still alive. **JOE?**

The idyllic years had ended for the Casey family of Dungarvan and the following evening, Dr Michael Augustine "Austie" Casey, 52, would, in his coffin, be removed by a relay of local factory workers whom he had employed in the Glue and Gelatine factory that he set up during the war, itself a bi-product of the tannery he had, in 1935, helped to establish in the centre of the town.

Funeral

Dungarvan shut down on the morning of the funeral and the place was so jammed that the car couldn't move through the crowd. Despite its size, the church couldn't accommodate all the mourners and hundreds had to stand in the precincts. Everyone could attend the burial immediately afterwards as the family plot was right by the entrance to the church. The people in attendance demonstrated the remarkably wide range of activities and contacts Austie had made in a life that paralleled perfectly the Irish nation in the first half of the twentieth century. A very large number in attendance would have been patients of Austie, for whom he had worked so painstakingly and conscientiously since his appointment as the local medical officer in **1932,** after a stint in nearby Cappoquin. There were the factory staff who had carried his body to the church the night before.

After that, the gathering was a diffuse, educated bunch, many of them leaders in the newly formed republic, hailing mostly from the East and South of the country. There were Austie's medical contacts, built up first in University College Dublin, where his studies overlapped with the Revolutionary Period of 1916-23, what he would have called The Troubles. His self-confessed involvement with the IRA in both Dublin and Waterford got him involved in politics and, in particular, Fianna Fail after their establishment and rise to power. It was through these contacts that, in 1935, he could organise the establishment of a large leather factory in Dungarvan, which Minister Sean Lemass would open. Several members attended from Dail Eireann and Seanad Eireann, along with officials from all public bodies in the country. The Waterford County Council members attended en bloc, as arranged at their emergency meeting on the Tuesday.

As a board member of two factories, Austie came into contact with many members of the legal and banking professions, and other managers and directors of various industrial concerns throughout the provinces of Munster and Leinster. It was through the work of such men that Ireland tried to fashion itself as a self-sufficient state, independent of Britain and scarcely connected by trade to Europe.

Austie's involvement in Gaelic games was honoured by the President of the GAA and very large attendance from the Gaels of Waterford, namely the people of the community. **Austie played a huge role in local games.** This era was the high point of Waterford hurling and football. They won the All-Ireland in 1948 and 1949, with Dungarvan being the bulk suppliers, and the Waterfod Foot

In attendance also were also Garda and Army representatives in attendance; the latter may have gotten to know Austie through his eldest brother, Fr. Richard, who had been Head Chaplain in the army until 1948.

Dick would have surely driven down from Skerries where he had, by his energetic standards, retired into a posting as Parish Priest, a role he kept until his death in 1962. It is highly unlikely, given his profession, that he was at home for Easter when Austie died, although he certainly would continue to be a regular guest in Mountain View.

Astonishingly, Dick was the celebrant of the mass (a **Solemn Requiem and High mass**) and was joined by an enormous array of local priests, inlcluding those from the parishes of Abbeyside, Old Parish. Ardmore

Dick was one of Austie's five surviving siblings. Joe and Fr Rennie were older while Percy and May were younger. **On this sad occasion,** Austie would be buried beside their little brother, John, who was only a few years younger than Austie but who had died aged 11, in 1917. **The first Michael died in infancy in 1892.** Joe, a highly successful accountant, had flown all the way from Los Angeles, where Austie and Anne had visited him on their tour of the States. Rennie had come from Lancashire where he worked as part of a mission among the large Irish community, although he would retire with illness and see out his days in Mountain View, later that decade. Percy had stayed local although his galavanting days were about to begin as he would step into Austie's shoes before also succumbing to a heart attack in 1957. Percy also ran a shop in the middle of the town which had been owned by their father, Michael J., the much-loved champion of the town's poor, until his death in 1923, and later taken over by his equally-loved wife, Catherine, until her death in 1940. **The gathering for Austie was perhaps the largest in the town since his mother died.**

## **Funeral**

Wednesday morning, 29 March, 1951

It's a **Wednesday** morning in late March and Dungarvan is dunta for the Doris Day. The busiest man in town has died and his funeral is today.

-   It's a curious irony that the now prosperous town has suspended business to celebrate the man who did more than anyone to bring work and wealth to the once-tough lives of people in a Free State town.

At his funeral today, it will be mentioned that Michael Augustine Casey, known as "Austie Casey", was "perhaps the greatest industrialist in Munster if not the country".

-   It's a big claim as he may not have even been the greatest leatherman to grace County Waterford in the early twentieth century – that award surely goes to Limerick's Kennedy O'Brien, who helped established tanneries in both Portlaw and Dungarvan, and elsewhere too.

    -   That honour perhaps belongs to Kennedy O'Brien, a *bona fide* leather man, who lived and breathed leather production from the age of *seventeen* when he began working in ?1907? in Ireland's last remaining big tannery.

-   But that perhaps only demonstrates the culture of Free State Eire at a time when the colonial aristocrats had been recently ousted and the industrial heartlands of the northern province had been partitioned off, leaving the body of an island without its industrious legs.

    -   The country had to bootstrap itself into a functional economic entity, led by a small, educated middle-class who would scramble to fill the new power vacuum, and **powered** by a class of labourers who were capable of hard, physical, and even noxious work.

-   Austie's biggest strength was neither on the factory floor nor in the day-to-day running of the business. He was the one who brought jobs to the people of Dungarvan, and not just seasonal work, as would have been common, but year-round work for the people of the town and countryside.
